questions.question_text: The vulnerability to conform is greater in individuals with which of the following characteristic features?
questions.explanation: People of high status more likely to induce conformity while people of low status more likely to conform. Conformity increases with increasing group size, but after five people the effect diminishes. People who are naive are more likely to conform, especially to members of their own group and less likely to conform to members of another group.

questions.question_text: Task completion is poor in which of the following types of leadership?
questions.explanation:
Contingency theories (also known as context theories and situational leadership) propose that there is no single best method for leadership, rather the situation will dictate the style and methodologies that need to be used, drawing on a toolkit of styles relevant to the context and followers at the time. In other words, successful leadership is determined both by the characteristics of the leader and the characteristics of the situation.

Psychologist Fred Fiedler was one of the first theorists to describe contingency theories. He proposed that a directive, authoritarian leadership style is most effective when circumstances are either very unfavourable or very favourable for the leader, and non-directive leadership is most effective in intermediate circumstances.

The three key factors determining the favourableness of the circumstances for the leader are leader-member relations (how much the leader is liked and respected by group members), position power (how much authority the leader has over group members), and task structure (how structured the group task is).

Autocratic, democratic and laissez-faire are leadership types proposed by Lewin. Productivity is higher in laissez-faire leadership than in autocratic leadership. Task completion is good in autocratic and democratic leaderships but poor in groups led by a leader with laissez-faire style.

questions.question_text: Which of the following correctly describes fundamental attribution error?

options.text: Refusing to accept one's own errors
Denying the fundamental flaws behind one's own negative behaviour
Attributing others' mistakes to the context in which the mistakes occur
Attributing one's own mistakes to one's character and personality
Attributing others' mistakes to their personal dispositions

correct_answer.text: Attributing others' mistakes to their personal dispositions

correct_answers.text: Attributing others' mistakes to their personal dispositions

questions.explanation: Fundamental attribution error is a pervasive tendency to underestimate the importance of external situational pressures and to overestimate the importance of internal motives and disposition in interpreting the behaviour of others. It is more pronounced if the attributed behaviour is negative and undesirable.

questions.question_text: Increased observation may lead to increased productivity in certain tasks. This is called the
questions.explanation: The Hawthorne effect refers to improvement in the performance or productivity of workers or students resulting from the introduction of new working methods or conditions, irrespective of the nature of the changes, the effect often being attributed to the feeling of being under concerned observation.

questions.question_text: An attitude scale has been constructed with the following response categories attached to each item - strongly disagree, disagree, neutral, agree, strongly agree. This is an example of a
questions.explanation: A Likert scale is a popular type of attitude scale, constructed by the method of 'summated ratings' in which a sample of respondents are given a number of candidate statements about an attitude object to which they respond with their own attitudes by choosing one of the response categories attached to each item, for example, strongly disagree, disagree, neutral, agree, strongly agree. Items that are worded positively toward the attitude object are assigned positively increasing scores to their response categories such as 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, respectively, and for negatively worded items the scoring is reversed (4, 3, 2, 1, 0).

questions.question_text: "Aggression is a consequence of frustration". Who proposed this hypothesis?
questions.explanation:
The frustration-aggression hypothesis is a conjecture originally put forward by the US psychologist John Dollard and four colleagues. In its strongest form, it states that the instigation to aggressive behaviour always presupposes frustration, and that frustration always leads to aggression.

According to Lorenz, aggression in nonhumans is essentially destructive and is characterised by ritualisation and appeasement. But in humans it is basically destructive and has become distorted. According to Berkowitz, aggressive-cue hypothesis frustration provokes anger, not aggression. For this anger to be expressed as aggression, certain environmental cues are needed.

questions.question_text: The power of a person due to his ability to provide something that is desired is known as
questions.explanation: Reward power is the power that is conveyed through rewarding individuals for compliance with one's wishes. This may be achieved through giving bonuses, raises, a promotion, and extra time off from work, etc. Coercive power is the power to punish. Referent power is the power through identification with the leader. Legitimate power is power bestowed by virtue of social position. Expert power is power resulting having greater knowledge or skills.

questions.question_text: The most common effect of cognitive dissonance is
questions.explanation:
Cognitive dissonance is a cognitive consistency theory, first proposed by psychologist Leon Festinger, concerned with the effects of inconsistent cognitions – interpreted as items of knowledge or belief. Dissonance is a motivating state of tension or distress that tends to generate three types of dissonance-reducing behaviour: changing one of the cognitions, decreasing the perceived importance of the dissonant cognitions, and/or adding further (justifying) cognitions.

The standard example of a dissonance relation is the pair of cognitions I smoke cigarettes and Cigarette smoking damages my health. People who hold both cognitions can reduce the dissonance in three ways: changing the first cognition by giving up smoking or convincing themselves that they have given up; changing the second cognition by rejecting, ignoring, or playing down the evidence linking cigarette smoking to ill health; or adding justifying cognitions such as But I only smoke low-tar brands or But I'm more likely to die in a car accident than from the effects of smoking - which is the easiest and commonest method of dissonance reduction.

questions.question_text: A candidate who has appeared for a mock exam before the actual exam scores better than a candidate who has not. This is called
questions.explanation: Practice effects occur when a participant in an experiment performs the same task twice or more after an interval. Subjects can either have a positive (subjects become better at performing the task) or negative (subjects become worse at performing the task) effect. Repeated measures designs are almost always affected by practice effects.

questions.question_text: The presence of others reduces task performance. This is called
questions.explanation: Social loafing is the tendency to exert less effort on a task when working as part of a cooperative group than when working on one's own – one reason why 'many hands make light work'. The phenomenon has been replicated across a variety of tasks, and evidence has shown that it is greatly reduced by making individual contributions identifiable within the group. Ringelmann demonstrated social loafing in the 1880s by observing tug-of-war teams. He demonstrated that the more people there were in a team, the less the effort made by each person in the team.

questions.question_text: In a social psychology experiment, an audience attended a convention where speakers were randomly allocated to speak in favour of or against an important political issue. The audience was told beforehand that the attitudes of the speakers were determined by a coin toss. Despite this, the subjects rated speakers who spoke in favour of the subject as having on average a more positive attitude towards the issue at stake than those who spoke against it. Which of the following does this indicate?
questions.explanation: Fundamental attribution error is a pervasive tendency to underestimate the importance of external situational pressures and to overestimate the importance of internal motives and disposition in interpreting the behaviour of others.

questions.question_text: The attributional bias hypothesised to contribute to persecutory delusions is
questions.explanation: It has been proposed that individuals with persecutory delusions make excessive external attributions for the cause of negative events. It remains unclear from empirical research findings whether the externalizing bias is also common to other psychotic symptom presentations.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is most likely to influence individuals to conform to the views of the group?

options.text: Individuals feel accepted by the group

questions.explanation: Ambiguous tasks tend to lead to more conformity as people may feel less certain of their own ideas.

questions.question_text: The theory of mind is not well developed in which of the following disorders?
questions.explanation: 'Theory of mind' refers to people's intuitive understanding of their own and other people's minds or mental states, including beliefs and thoughts. People with autistic spectrum disorder are severely impaired in their ability to understand mental states and to appreciate how mental states govern behaviour. Children typically develop the theory of mind around four years of age.

questions.question_text: At what age do children pass the mirror test?
questions.explanation: Mirror test- A test for self-recognition in which the child using its mirror image to touch a dot on its nose is achieved at 18 months of age.

questions.question_text: Which of the following accurately reflects instrumental aggression?

options.text: It is carried out using destructive weapons
It is motivated by negative feelings

questions.explanation: Instrumental aggression is carried out for the purpose of achieving a particular goal, e.g., kidnapping for ransom. Hence, it is often planned and not impulsive. Hostile (also called angry or affective) aggression is motivated by the need to express negative feelings, such as anger.

questions.question_text: In a small group situation, under which of the following conditions departures from norms are most likely to be tolerated?

options.text: The norms were stated frequently during previous meetings
Dissent comes from a member with strong credentials
A consensus was reached before the dissent was expressed

correct_answer.text: Dissent comes from a member with strong credentials

correct_answers.text: Dissent comes from a member with strong credentials

questions.explanation: Group members may wish to ignore a norm if it is burdensome or a source of punishment. Norm rejection is more easily achieved in the absence of enforcement and more readily tolerated if the rejecting member possesses strengths and abilities needed by the group. A norm that has been frequently and clearly stated is more difficult to avoid because members cannot then claim ignorance or misinterpretation. The threat of censure or punishment is a strong deter- rent to violation of group norms, especially if the group is very cohesive and if the setting is one of privacy.

questions.question_text: What factor is the most influential in the development of friendly relationships?
questions.explanation: A classic study of beginning friendship was reported by Theodore Newcomb in The Acquaintance Process (1961). Newcomb identified four factors that affect the probability of making an acquaintance. 1. Proximity. We are more likely to get to know somebody with whom we have regular contact. 2. Reciprocity. We like people who like us.3. Similarity. We like people who share our values and beliefs. 4. Complementarity. We are attracted to people whose skills and abilities are complementary to our own. Complementary means different but compatible and mutually beneficial, like people with different skills who work together for a common purpose. (From Dewey, RA. Chapter 16: Friendship from Psychology: An Introduction, http://www.intropsych.com/ch16_sfl/friendship.html).

questions.question_text: The pressure to conform with one's group is reduced if

options.text: There is some dissent expressed within the group
The situation is ambiguous and it is unclear how one should respond
Group members are perceived to be socially influential
All of the group members belong to a collectivist culture

correct_answer.text: There is some dissent expressed within the group

correct_answers.text: There is some dissent expressed within the group

questions.explanation: Conformity refers to the normative social influence that makes an individual to agree with the group view despite holding a different personal view. Experiments by Asch using a line length judging task in a group setting explained various features of conformity seen in social settings. Conformity increases with group number (maximum effect with three) and the perceived high status of other group members. Less intelligent members conform more than those with higher IQ. The presence of dissent in the group reduces conformity. People from collectivist cultures are more (not less) likely to conform. People are also more likely to conform in ambiguous situations (i.e. when it is not clear how one should proceed).

questions.question_text: In a dark room, several lights are turned on and off in rapid succession. An observer perceives a single light as moving from one position to the next rather than different lights coming on and off at different positions. What is this called?
questions.explanation: As defined by the psychologist Max Wertheimer, the phi phenomenon (also called phi movement) is a form of pure objectless apparent movement, without the appearance of any entity actually moving, that occurs when two visual stimuli a few centimeters apart are presented in an alternating pattern with an interstimulus interval too long for the stimuli to appear simultaneous or for partial movement or optimal movement to occur, but not long enough for the disappearance of apparent movement and the veridical perception of the stimuli simply alternating. The term is often applied to any form of apparent movement.

questions.question_text: Which of the following factors reduce cognitive dissonance?

options.text: Adding one or more justifying cognitions

correct_answer.text: Adding one or more justifying cognitions

correct_answers.text: Adding one or more justifying cognitions

questions.question_text: A depressed patient has shown a good degree of improvement in her sleep pattern after initiating a new treatment. Though objectively she continues to be depressed, when using a self-rated scale to monitor her symptoms, she significantly overrates the degree of improvement in her mood and other domains. This effect is called
questions.explanation: The halo effect is a generalisation from the perception of one prominent or salient characteristic, trait, or personality attribute to an impression of the whole, leading to inflated correlations between rated items. This phenomenon is well established in the study of physical attractiveness. More positive personality traits are often ascribed to individuals who are more attractive.

questions.question_text: The first aspect of self-concept to develop is the
questions.explanation: Bodily self-refers to the ability to differentiate one's own body from that of others.

questions.question_text: Which one among the following is defined by how much we approve of ourselves and how worthy we think of ourselves?
questions.explanation:
Self-esteem is one's attitude towards oneself or one's opinion or evaluation of oneself, which may be positive (favourable or high), neutral, or negative (unfavourable or low).

Self-image may be defined as the way we think we are like and how we describe ourselves. Self-efficacy is a term referring to the belief that we can perform adequately in a given situation. Self-awareness is the state of being or ability to be, consciously aware of oneself. Humans and other great apes are believed to have this capacity. Self-actualisation is the motive to realise one's full potential. According to Maslow's theory, self-actualised people have an acceptance of who they are despite their faults and limitations and experience a drive to be creative in all aspects of their lives.

questions.question_text: A patient feels unhappy with respect to one aspect of his life. Soon he observes that this unhappiness affects several other aspects of his life as well, resulting in a depressed state of mind. Which of the following types of cognitive bias is most likely to be relevant to this description?
questions.explanation:
Domino effect is the psychological equivalent of the butterfly effect in chaos theory. According to this notion, large changes within a system or structure often depends on the initial conditions in which a small change can result in a large catastrophe.

When a person in a depressed state of mind starts to classify events in negative concepts, these concepts become proliferated with instances and start bearing resemblances to many more things which become categorized negatively, adding yet more instances. This vicious cycle or domino effect is characteristic of rumination or repetitive thoughts in mood disorders.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a behavioural component of Allport's concept of prejudice?
questions.explanation: Prejudice is essentially an attitude. Hence, it has 1. Cognitive component - stereotypes; 2. Affective component - hostility; 3. Behavioural component - which according to Allport can be Anti-locution, avoidance, discrimination. physical attack or extermination in terms of increasing severity.

questions.question_text: Individuals often tend not to intervene when someone seeks help, especially when others who can offer help are present in the vicinity. In social psychology, this phenomenon is known as
questions.explanation: 'Diffusion of responsibility' is a reduced sense of interpersonal responsibility and individual accountability experienced in certain circumstances by members of a group, often leading to behaviour that is not typical of any of the group members when alone. It is related to the 'bystander effect' (also known as the 'Genovese syndrome') which is the reluctance of bystanders to intervene in an emergency, especially when a person appears to be in distress or a crime is being committed. Scores of experiments have shown that people are much less likely to intervene in an emergency, and are generally slower to respond, when other people are present than when they are alone, and this phenomenon is sometimes called 'group inhibition of helping' or 'bystander apathy effect'. In pluralistic ignorance, members of a group convince each other that there is no problem that requires intervention.

options.text: Method of choice for solving abstract problems

questions.question_text: Attitudes do not always correlate with one's behaviours. The attitudes that most accurately predict behaviour are those that are

options.text: Not based on one's own life experiences

questions.explanation: Attitudes predict behaviour if 1. They are strong and consistent 2.Based on direct experience and 3. Specifically relate to the behaviour being predicted.

questions.question_text: The classic studies by Milgram explain the concept of
questions.explanation: The Milgram experiment is a famous experimental procedure introduced in 1963 by the US psychologist Stanley Milgram to study obedience to authority. Milgram conducted a series of experiments in which approximately two-thirds of participants ('teachers') administered what they believed to be extremely painful and possibly lethal electric shocks to an innocent victim ('learner') when instructed to do so by an authoritative experimenter ('experimenter'). Factors proposed to influence obedience include proximity of experimenter to teacher, both indirectness and proximity of learner to teacher ('teacher' less likely to obey if the victim was closer), authority of the situation (institutional authority), authority or status of the experimenter, and group pressure (there was a liberating effect of disobedient peers).

questions.question_text: According to the frustration-aggression hypothesis which of the following is false?

options.text: Aggression is the one of the many possible responses to frustration
Fear of punishment can inhibit aggression
Aggression is driven by a need to nullify frustration
Unavailability of the frustrator can inhibit aggression
Unexpressed frustration cannot be displaced onto an innocent target

correct_answer.text: Unexpressed frustration cannot be displaced onto an innocent target

correct_answers.text: Unexpressed frustration cannot be displaced onto an innocent target

questions.explanation: The frustration-aggression hypothesis of Dollard considers aggression to be one of the many possible products of frustration. In a meta-analysis including 49 studies, Marcus-Newhall, Pedersen, Carlson and Miller (2000) found consistent evidence that frustrated individuals show displacement of aggression from the source of the frustration onto a less powerful or more accessible target.

questions.question_text: Which of the following increases the effectiveness of a persuasive communication?
questions.explanation: In social psychology, the persuasiveness of a person or message source is generally associated with credibility or prestige. Carl Hovland, at Yale University, studied various factors affecting persuasion. The credibility of a perceived message is a crucial factor in persuasion (Hovland and Weiss, 1951); a health report is more persuasive if it is published in a professional medical journal than in a tabloid.

questions.question_text: In Milgram's obedience experiments, the factors that increased obedience include all except

options.text: Relieving the subject from responsibility of actions

questions.question_text: Which of the following can reduce groupthink?
questions.explanation:
Groupthink is a collective pattern of defensive avoidance, characteristic of group decision making in organisations in which group members develop rationalisations supporting shared illusions of their own infallibility and invulnerability within the organisation. Characteristic features include: an illusion of invulnerability; collective efforts to rationalise in order to discount warnings; an unquestioned belief in the group's inherent morality; stereotyped views of rivals and enemies; direct pressure on any member who dissents from the consensus view; self-censorship of disagreements with the apparent group consensus; a shared illusion of unanimity; and the emergence of self-appointed protectors of the group from adverse information that might undermine the existing complacency.

Various strategies that can reduce groupthink include encouraging open debate, acknowledging the presence of groupthink, seeking external opinion, splitting the group into smaller units for discussion, holding last chance meetings to encourage challenges, and reserving the leader's opinions until after the group's discussion has been completed.

questions.question_text: Tom is a student who attributes a good grade on an exam to his intelligence and hard work but a poor grade to the teacher's poor ability and unfair test questions. He is exhibiting
questions.explanation: Self-serving bias is an attributional bias that leads people to ascribe their own successes to internal personal factors, such as ability, and their failures to external situational causes, such as bad luck. This bias is a mechanism for individuals to protect or enhance their own selfesteem.

options.text: "I have more chances of dying when crossing a road than injecting cocaine"
"Smoking is worse killer than cocaine use"
"Alcohol affects the whole body while cocaine is not that bad"
"Even Freud used cocaine in those days, there must be something good about it"

options.text: A person attributes other people's behaviour to internal sources
A person attributes other people's behaviour to external sources
A person attributes successes to external sources
A person attributes successes to internal sources
A person attributes failures to internal sources

correct_answer.text: A person attributes successes to internal sources

correct_answers.text: A person attributes successes to internal sources

questions.explanation: Self-serving bias is an attributional bias that leads people to ascribe their own successes to internal personal factors, such as ability, and their failures to external situational causes, such as bad luck.

questions.question_text: A mother of an autistic child is curious to know the reason behind her son's apparent lack of empathy towards other children of similar age. Which of the following concept is relevant to address her question?
questions.explanation: 'Theory of mind' refers to people's intuitive understanding of their own and other people's minds or mental states, including beliefs and thoughts. People with autistic spectrum disorder are severely impaired in their ability to understand mental states and to appreciate how mental states govern behaviour.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is true concerning primate psychology?

options.text: Aggressive male baboons have longer life expectancy
Aggression is higher during periods of instability
Young baboons learn appropriate expression of aggression by observing their peers
Low ranking baboons are not aggressive
Among baboons, females are not aggressive

correct_answer.text: Aggression is higher during periods of instability

correct_answers.text: Aggression is higher during periods of instability

questions.explanation: During periods of instability such as rank transition, baboons show higher levels of aggression. This leads to high cortisol levels and stress among the animals.

questions.question_text: A team leader is constantly calling for her group to focus on its commitment to the overall outcomes more than anything else. She is keen to ensure that all opinions are heard, and decisions made are satisfactory to most of the team. She is following a
questions.explanation: Persuasion is the ability to motivate and enthuse the group to pursue the goal. It differs from coercion where power is used to enforce change through rewards and punishment. Modern leadership is the very antithesis of coercion because it involves a degree of consensus rather than blind obedience.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following is a secondary drive?
questions.explanation:
A drive is any internal source of motivation that impels an organism to pursue a goal or to satisfy a need, such as sex, hunger, or self-preservation.
In theories of motivation, Mowrer distinguished between primary and secondary drives.
A primary drive is an innate physiological urge or need, such as hunger, thirst, or the need for sex. A secondary drive is an acquired non-physiological urge, such as the need for achievement or the need for affiliation (e.g. money, play).
While primary drives come and go, secondary drives are often continuous.

questions.question_text: Scapegoating refers to

options.text: Tension between racial groups rise when the economic conditions are similar
Encouraging conflicts with a political motive
Sexual assault on a vulnerable group leading to conflicts
Lack of empathy on perpetrators of abuse
Captives becoming emotionally attached to the captivators

correct_answer.text: Tension between racial groups rise when the economic conditions are similar

correct_answers.text: Tension between racial groups rise when the economic conditions are similar

questions.explanation: Scapegoats are singled out victims who are blamed and discriminated by virtue of their group membership (e.g. racial group, work group, etc.). Scapegoating involves political and economic factors as well. Under the economic and political competition model, when resources are relatively scarce, the dominant group in society will try to exploit [people from underrepresented groups] for material gain. Discrimination and prejudice are heightened during times of tension and increased competition over limited resources. Hovland and Sears showed that between 1882 and 1930, there was a direct relationship between the price of cotton and the number of lynchings of Blacks. As the price of cotton decreased, the number of lynchings increased. In the aftermath of the Tokyo Earthquake of 1923, which claimed the lives of 100,000 people, several thousand Koreans were said to be massacred. The racial hatred allegedly stemmed from the competition from the influx of Korean labor for scarce jobs that were available.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is considered to be a factor of social influence when a group makes a polarized decision?
questions.explanation: Normative influence: People have a need not to appear odd or 'stick out' as a sore thumb. So we say yes often to what the others say.

questions.question_text: The semantic differential scale may be subject to which of the following problems?
questions.explanation: The semantic differential scale is a visual analogue scale (7 points) with two polarized adjectives at either extremes separated by a line. The subjects mark their attitudes between the two. It may be subject to positional response bias.

questions.question_text: Which of the following concepts refers to the loss of the sense of individuality and a submerging of personal identity and accountability in a group setting?
questions.explanation:
Deindividuation is a psychological state characterised by loss of the sense of individuality and a submerging of personal identity and accountability in a group (i.e, anonymity). In some circumstances it can lead to a relaxation of inhibitions and the release of antisocial behaviour, and it has been used to explain certain forms of mob behaviour (e.g. riots). The larger the group, the greater the anonymity and the greater the difficulty in identifying a single individual.

Polarization refers to the social phenomenon wherein individuals express 'moderate' opinions when asked one-to-one, but as a group make more extreme decision on the same issue. Risky shift phenomenon: people tend to make riskier decisions when working as members of a group than they would make when making the same decision as individuals. Sociogram developed by Moreno is a graphical representation of relationships in a group.
